questions.stem: In a system, numbers are represented using 4-bit two’s complement form. Consider four numbers $N_1 = 1011$, $N_2 = 1101$, $N_3 = 1010$ and $N_4 = 1001$ in the system. Which of the following operations will result in arithmetic overflow?

steps.title: Define the range and what overflow means
steps.body: Two's complement with $n$ bits stores an integer $v$ as the bit pattern of $v \bmod 2^n$. The leftmost bit has weight $-2^{n-1}$ and every other bit $+2^i$, so the representable values are exactly $-2^{n-1}$ to $2^{n-1}-1$. Overflow means the true arithmetic result falls outside that range, so the $n$-bit pattern would show a wrong value. With $n = 4$ the range is $-8$ to $+7$. We compute each true result as an ordinary integer and test it against this range.

steps.title: Evaluate each operation against $[-8, 7]$
steps.body: (A) $-5 + (-3) = -8$, inside the range (it is the pattern 1000). (B) $-3 + (-6) = -9$, below $-8$: overflow. (C) $-6 - (-7) = 1$, inside. (D) $-5 + (-7) = -12$, below $-8$: overflow.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Overflow happens in B and D, so the answer is options B and D.

shortcut.body: Adding two negatives overflows when the sum is below $-8$, that is when their magnitudes add to more than 8. $5+3 = 8$ is fine, $3+6 = 9$ and $5+7 = 12$ are not. Subtracting a negative adds a positive, so C cannot overflow here. Safe for any width: compare the true sum to the range.

traps.text: Option A gives exactly $-8$. It is the most negative value and still fits, so calling it overflow is the off-by-one slip.
Option C looks like a subtraction of two large numbers, but $N_3 - N_4 = -6 + 7 = 1$. Subtracting a negative number adds, it never pushes the result to an extreme.

recognize.clues: Four named 4-bit patterns and the wording "which operations result in arithmetic overflow" point to testing each exact result against the representable range.
recognize.contrast: twos-complement only converts between patterns and values; here decoding is the first step and the real task is the range test, where a result sitting exactly on the lowest value still fits.

check.body: Second route, by carries: overflow happens exactly when the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of it. For 1101 + 1010 the carry into the sign bit is 0 and the carry out is 1, so it overflows (the 4-bit pattern 0111 would read $+7$ instead of $-9$). For 1011 + 1101 both carries are 1, and the pattern 1000 correctly reads $-8$.

questions.stem: The 32-bit IEEE 754 single precision representation of a number is 0xC2710000. The number in decimal representation is ________. (rounded off to two decimal places)

solutionDiagram.alt: The hex word 0xC2710000 split into sign 1, exponent 10000100 and fraction 1110001, then the steps to the value minus 60.25.

steps.title: Define the single-precision layout
steps.body: IEEE 754 single precision uses 32 bits: 1 sign bit $s$, an 8-bit exponent field $e$ read as an unsigned number, and a 23-bit fraction $f$. For a normal number ($0 < e < 255$) the value is $(-1)^s \times 1.f \times 2^{e-127}$. The leading 1 before the point is not stored (the hidden bit), and 127 is the bias subtracted from $e$ to allow negative exponents.

steps.title: Split the hex into bits and fields
steps.body: C2710000 in binary is 1100 0010 0111 0001 0000 0000 0000 0000. The first bit is the sign: $s = 1$, so the number is negative. The next eight bits are 1000 0100, so $e = 132$. The remaining 23 bits are 1110001 followed by sixteen zeros.

steps.title: Remove the bias
steps.body: The true exponent is $132 - 127 = 5$. The significand is $1.1110001_2 = 1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \tfrac1{64} = 1.8828125$.

steps.title: Compute and finish
steps.body: Moving the point five places right gives $111100.01_2 = 60 + 0.25 = 60.25$. With the sign bit set the value is $-60.25$, already exact to two decimals.

shortcut.body: Read the exponent from the first three hex digits: C27 means sign 1 and exponent 1000 0100 = 132, so $2^5$. Then the leading hex digits of the fraction, 71 = 0111 0001, give the first bits 1110001 after the hidden 1: $1.1110001 \times 32 = 111100.01$. About one minute.

traps.text: Forgetting the hidden 1 gives $0.1110001 \times 32 = 28.25$, and forgetting the sign gives $+60.25$.
Using bias 128 gives exponent $4$, and the answer becomes $-30.125$. Bias 126 gives exponent $6$ and $-120.5$.

recognize.clues: A 32-bit hex word described as IEEE 754 single precision, with the decimal value asked for: split it into sign, exponent and fraction, then apply the bias and the hidden 1.
recognize.contrast: ieee754-special matters only when the exponent field is all zeros or all ones. Here it is neither, so the ordinary normal-number formula applies.

check.body: Re-encode the result. $60.25 = 111100.01_2 = 1.1110001_2 \times 2^5$, so the sign bit is 1, the exponent field is $5+127 = 132 = 1000\,0100$ and the fraction is 1110001 followed by zeros. Regrouping in fours gives 1100 0010 0111 0001 0000 ..., which is the word C2710000 from the question.

questions.stem: Consider the 8-bit signed integers $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ represented using the sign-magnitude form. The binary representations of $X$ and $Y$ are as follows: $X$: 10110100, $Y$: 01001100. Which of the following operations to compute $Z$ result(s) in an arithmetic overflow?

steps.title: Define sign-magnitude and its range
steps.body: In sign-magnitude form the leftmost bit is the sign (1 means negative) and the other bits are the magnitude as an ordinary binary number. With 8 bits the magnitude has 7 bits, so it is at most $127$ and the representable values are $-127$ to $+127$. Overflow means the true result has magnitude above 127.

steps.title: Decode X and Y
steps.body: $X = 10110100$ has sign 1 and magnitude $0110100_2 = 52$, so $X = -52$. $Y = 01001100$ has sign 0 and magnitude $1001100_2 = 76$, so $Y = +76$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: B and C exceed $\pm 127$, so the answer is options B and C. Note that $-128$ would fit in two’s complement but sign-magnitude has no code for it.

shortcut.body: Overflow needs two operands of the same effective sign: B is $(-52) + (-76)$ and C is $(+52) + (+76)$. Both magnitudes add to $128 > 127$. A and D mix signs, so the result is smaller than either operand and cannot overflow. Takes 30 seconds.

traps.text: Treating the range as $-128$ to $127$ (two’s complement habit) would make B look legal. Sign-magnitude loses $-128$.
Calling A overflow because both bit patterns look large ignores the sign bit of X: it makes $X$ negative, so A is $76 - 52$.

recognize.clues: The words "sign-magnitude form" and "arithmetic overflow" for X+Y, X-Y, -X+Y and -X-Y: decode the two inputs, apply the signs, and test the magnitude of each result.
recognize.contrast: signed-representations teaches the sign-magnitude encoding itself, and here it is only the first step. Unlike two’s complement, the range is symmetric, so the extra low value of two’s complement does not exist.

check.body: Test magnitudes only. Operands of opposite effective sign subtract their magnitudes, so the result cannot exceed the larger input, 76. Operands of the same effective sign add magnitudes, $52+76 = 128$, which needs the 8-bit magnitude 1000 0000, more than the 7 magnitude bits 111 1111 = 127 can hold.

questions.stem: Consider the real valued variables X, Y and Z represented using the IEEE 754 single-precision floating-point format. The binary representations of X and Y in hexadecimal notation are as follows: X: 35C00000, Y: 34A00000. Let $Z = X + Y$. Which one of the following is the binary representation of $Z$, in hexadecimal notation?

solutionDiagram.alt: Decode of X and Y, shifting Y right by two places to match exponent 107, adding the significands to 1.1101 and reading off 0x35E80000.

steps.title: Define the format and the rule for adding
steps.body: A single-precision normal number is $(-1)^s \times 1.f \times 2^{e-127}$ with 1 sign bit, an 8-bit exponent field $e$ and a 23-bit fraction $f$ (the leading 1 is implied). To add two such numbers the hardware shifts the one with the smaller exponent right until both exponents agree, adds the significands, then renormalises so the result again has the form $1.f$.

steps.title: Align the exponents
steps.body: The exponents differ by $107 - 105 = 2$, so shift $Y$ right two places: $1.01_2 \times 2^{-22} = 0.0101_2 \times 2^{-20}$. No bits fall off the 23-bit fraction, so nothing is lost.

steps.title: Add the significands
steps.body: $1.1000_2 + 0.0101_2 = 1.1101_2$. This is already of the form $1.f$, so there is no renormalising and the exponent stays 107.

steps.title: Write the result back as hex
steps.body: Sign 0, exponent 0110 1011, fraction 1101 000... (23 bits, the 4 significant fraction bits 1101 then zeros). The 32 bits are 0 01101011 11010000000000000000000 = 0011 0101 1110 1000 0000 ... = 0x35E80000, which is option C.

shortcut.body: The exponents are 107 and 105, so the sum keeps exponent 107 (the significand sum stays below 2, so there is no carry) and the first hex digits stay 35. Only the top fraction bits change: $1.5 + 1.25/4 = 1.8125 = 1.1101_2$, so the fraction starts 1101 and the word is 35E8 0000. Options A, B and D decode to significands 1.5625, 1.59375 and 1.84375, none of them 1.8125.

traps.text: 35C80000 decodes to significand $1.5625$, so $Y$ would have contributed only $0.0625$ instead of $0.3125$. That is the result of dropping the hidden 1 of $Y$ (using $0.01_2 = 0.25$ instead of $1.01_2 = 1.25$) before shifting it right two places.

35CC0000 decodes to significand $1.59375$, so $Y$ would have contributed $0.09375$ instead of $0.3125$. Its fraction bits are 1001 1, not 1101, so it is not the aligned sum. The true contribution is $1.25 / 4 = 0.3125$.

35EC0000 decodes to significand $1.84375 = 1.5 + 0.34375$. That is $0.03125$ more than the true sum $1.8125$: the fifth fraction bit is set where it should be clear, so the fraction reads 1101 1 instead of 1101 0.
Not aligning the exponents and adding $1.1 + 1.01 = 10.11$ gives the exponent field 108, so the word starts 0x36 instead of 0x35. Adding $1.5 + 1.25 = 2.75$ is the same mistake.

recognize.clues: Two hex words in IEEE 754 single precision and a request for the hex word of their sum: decode both, align the exponents, add, then encode again.
recognize.contrast: Adding the two 32-bit words as integers is wrong, because the exponent and the hidden 1 make a floating-point sum something other than a bitwise sum.

check.body: Scale everything by $2^{-22}$. Then $X = 6 \times 2^{-22}$ and $Y = 1.25 \times 2^{-22}$, so $Z = 7.25 \times 2^{-22} = 1.8125 \times 2^{-20}$. The significand 1.8125 needs only four fraction bits, so nothing is rounded away, and the exponent field stays 107 = 0110 1011 with fraction 1101 followed by zeros, which encodes as 0x35E80000.

questions.stem: The following two signed 2’s complement numbers (multiplicand $M$ and multiplier $Q$) are being multiplied using Booth’s algorithm: $M$: 1100 1101 1110 1101 and $Q$: 1010 0100 1010 1010. The total number of addition and subtraction operations to be performed is ___________. (Answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: The multiplier bits with the extra zero, each adjacent pair labelled as subtract M, add M or no operation, ending with 7 subtractions and 6 additions.

steps.title: Define Booth’s rule
steps.body: Booth’s algorithm multiplies two’s complement numbers by scanning the multiplier $Q$ from the right, one bit at a time. An extra bit $q_{-1} = 0$ sits to the right of $Q$. At step $i$ the pair $(q_i, q_{i-1})$ decides the action: 00 or 11 means only shift; 01 means add $M$ (the end of a run of 1s); 10 means subtract $M$ (the start of a run of 1s). The question counts adds plus subtracts, not shifts.

steps.title: Write Q with the extra bit
steps.body: Q = 1010 0100 1010 1010 and the appended bit $q_{-1} = 0$ give the 17 symbols 1 0 1 0 0 1 0 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 0. Each step looks at a bit $q_i$ and the bit to its right, $q_{i-1}$. An operation happens exactly where those two bits differ.

steps.title: Count and check
steps.body: Subtractions occur at $i = 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 13, 15$, which is 7. Additions occur at $i = 2, 4, 6, 8, 11, 14$, which is 6. Total $7 + 6 = 13$. Check: the 13 shifted terms sum to $M \times Q = (-12819)(-23382) = 299733858$.

shortcut.body: Write Q with the extra 0 on the right and count the runs of equal bits: 1 | 0 | 1 | 00 | 1 | 00 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 00 is 14 runs, so there are 13 places where neighbouring bits differ, and each is one addition or subtraction. Only Q matters; $M$ never changes the count. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Counting the 1s of Q (7 of them) or only the 01 pairs (6) misses that every run of 1s costs a subtract at its start and an add at its end.
Counting the 16 shifts as operations gives 16. That is the number of cycles, not the number of additions and subtractions.
Leaving out the appended $q_{-1} = 0$ loses the pair at $i = 0$; here it is 00 so the count survives, but with a multiplier ending in 1 it would drop an operation.

recognize.clues: Two 16-bit two’s complement numbers multiplied with Booth’s algorithm, and the question counts additions and subtractions: that count depends only on the bit pattern of the multiplier.
recognize.contrast: The number of shift cycles is always 16, the width, and plain shift-and-add adds once per 1 bit. Neither is the Booth count, which charges per run of 1s.

check.body: Count by runs of 1s. Q contains seven 1s and none is adjacent to another, so there are seven runs. Each run costs a subtraction at its start and an addition just above its end, which is 14 operations. The run at the top bit has no position above it inside the 16 bits, so its addition never happens: $14 - 1 = 13$.

questions.stem: The number $-6$ can be represented as 1010 in 4-bit 2’s complement representation. Which of the following is/are CORRECT 2’s complement representation(s) of $-6$?

steps.title: Define two’s complement and sign extension
steps.body: Two’s complement with $n$ bits stores an integer $v$ as the bit pattern of $v \bmod 2^n$. The leftmost bit has weight $-2^{n-1}$ and every other bit has weight $+2^i$. To write the same number with more bits you copy the sign bit into all the new leftmost positions; this is called sign extension.

steps.title: Why copying the sign bit preserves the value
steps.body: Extending an $n$-bit negative number by one more 1 on the left changes the old sign bit’s weight from $-2^{n-1}$ to $+2^{n-1}$ and gives the new leftmost bit weight $-2^{n}$. Because $-2^{n} + 2^{n-1} = -2^{n-1}$, the total is unchanged. A leading 0 would instead make the number positive.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The correct extensions are the ones padded with 1s: B and D.

shortcut.body: Sign-extend 1010 by copying the leading 1: the correct wide forms are 1111 1010 and 1111 1111 1111 1010, so pick the options whose new bits are all 1s. Options padded with 0s after a leading 1 (A, C) are not extensions. Ten seconds.

traps.text: Options A and C pad the middle with zeros while putting a 1 on the far left, which is sign-magnitude style thinking, not two’s complement. They decode to $-118$ and $-32758$.

recognize.clues: "Correct 2’s complement representation(s) of $-6$" in 8 and 16 bits: the same value written at a wider width, which is sign extension.
recognize.contrast: Sign-magnitude widens by inserting zeros after the sign bit, while two’s complement copies the sign bit into every new position. Mixing the two habits is what the wrong options do.

check.body: Second route, by modular value. The 8-bit pattern of $-6$ is $2^8 - 6 = 250 = 1111\,1010_2$ and the 16-bit pattern is $2^{16} - 6 = 65530 = 1111\,1111\,1111\,1010_2$. Both agree with the sign-extended forms.

questions.stem: The format of a single-precision floating-point number as per the IEEE 754 standard is: Sign (1 bit), Exponent (8 bits), Mantissa (23 bits). Choose the largest floating-point number among the following options.

steps.title: Define the format and the reserved exponent
steps.body: A single-precision word is sign, 8-bit exponent field $e$ and 23-bit mantissa (fraction) $f$. For $1 \le e \le 254$ it is a normal number $(-1)^s \times 1.f \times 2^{e-127}$. The exponent field $e = 255$ (all ones) is reserved: fraction 0 means infinity, and any nonzero fraction means NaN (not a number). NaN is not a number at all, so it cannot be the largest number.

steps.title: Classify the four options
steps.body: A: $e = 127$, so $2^0 \times 1.111\ldots1 \approx 2 - 2^{-23}$, just under 2. B: $e = 254$, so $2^{127} \times (2 - 2^{-23})$, about $3.4 \times 10^{38}$. C: $e = 255$ with a nonzero fraction, which is NaN. D: $e = 127$, fraction 0, so exactly 1.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: NaN (C) is not comparable. Among the numbers, the exponent dominates: $2^{127}$ against $2^0$, so B is the largest. B is also the largest finite single-precision value.

shortcut.body: Look only at the exponent fields: 1111 1111 is NaN here, so skip it; 1111 1110 is the biggest legal exponent, so B wins without computing anything.

traps.text: Option C has the biggest bit pattern, but all-ones exponent with a nonzero fraction is NaN, not a number, so it is not the largest.
Option A has the largest mantissa but a tiny exponent; its value is about 2, far below $2^{127}$.
Option D is exactly 1, the smallest of the valid numbers listed.

questions.stem: Consider a system that uses 5 bits for representing signed integers in 2’s complement format. In this system, two integers $A$ and $B$ are represented as $A = 01010$ and $B = 11010$. steps.title: Define the range
steps.body: Two's complement with $n$ bits stores an integer $v$ as the bit pattern of $v \bmod 2^n$. The leftmost bit has weight $-2^{n-1}$ and every other bit $+2^i$, so the representable values are exactly $-2^{n-1}$ to $2^{n-1}-1$. Overflow means the true arithmetic result falls outside that range, so the $n$-bit pattern would show a wrong value. Overflow is a result above the top of the range, underflow a result below the bottom. With $n = 5$ the range is $-16$ to $+15$.

steps.title: Evaluate each operation
steps.body: (A) $A + B = 4$, fits. (B) $A - B = 10 + 6 = 16$, above 15: overflow. (C) $B - A = -16$, equals the bottom of the range, fits. (D) $2B = -12$, fits.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only $A - B = 16$ leaves $[-16, 15]$, so the answer is option B.

shortcut.body: Decode to 10 and $-6$. The only result that can leave the range is the one with the largest magnitude: $10 + 6 = 16 > 15$. Option C is $-16$, which is exactly the minimum and fits.

traps.text: $A + B$ adds a positive and a negative number, so the result lies between the two operands and cannot overflow: $10 - 6 = 4$.
$B - A = -6 - 10 = -16$ is the most negative 5-bit value (10000). Calling it underflow is the off-by-one slip: the range is asymmetric, $-16$ to $+15$.
$2 * B = -12$, inside the range. Doubling is a left shift, and it overflows only when the top two bits of $B$ differ; here they are 11, so the sign is kept.

recognize.clues: The phrase "arithmetic overflow or arithmetic underflow" over fixed-width 2's complement operands, with four expressions to test, means comparing true results with the n-bit range.
recognize.contrast: Not a number-representation question about reading a single pattern (twos-complement); here the operations are the point, and a subtraction or a doubling can overflow even when the operands themselves are small.

check.body: Do the subtraction in hardware style. A - B is A + (NOT B) + 1 = 01010 + 00101 + 1 = 10000. Both addends are non-negative in 5 bits yet the result has sign bit 1, so the sign flipped from the operands: overflow. Run the same method on B - A: 11010 + 10101 + 1 = 1 10000, and with the carry dropped the sign agrees with both negative addends, so no overflow.

questions.stem: Consider the IEEE-754 single precision floating point numbers P = 0xC1800000 and Q = 0x3F5C2EF4. Which one of the following corresponds to the product of these numbers (i.e., $P \times Q$), represented in the IEEE-754 single precision format?

steps.title: Define the format and the product rule
steps.body: A normal single-precision number is $(-1)^s \times 1.f \times 2^{e-127}$ with 1 sign bit, an 8-bit exponent field $e$ and a 23-bit fraction $f$. The product of two such numbers has sign equal to the XOR of the signs, significand equal to the product of the significands and exponent equal to the sum of the true exponents. If the new significand reaches 2 or more it is shifted right once and the exponent rises by 1.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: Because $P$ has significand exactly 1.0, the product keeps the fraction of $Q$ unchanged. The sign is negative. The true exponent is $4 + (-1) = 3$, so the exponent field is $3 + 127 = 130 = 1000\,0010_2$.

shortcut.body: P is a power of two ($-16$, significand 1.0), so the product changes only the sign and the exponent and leaves the fraction 5C2EF4 alone. The sign must be negative, so the word starts with C and A, B are out. The exponent is $127 + 4 - 1 = 130 = 0x82$, so the first byte is 1 1000 0010 giving C1: only option C.

traps.text: Option A starts 0x40: sign 0 and exponent field 128. It is positive although $P$ is negative, and its fraction 4C2EF4 differs from that of $Q$.
Option B keeps the fraction 5C2EF4 but its sign bit is 0 and its exponent field is 128 (true exponent 1). The product of a negative and a positive is negative, and the exponent is $4 + (-1) = 3$.
Option D has the right sign and exponent but fraction 4C2EF4 instead of 5C2EF4. Multiplying by $1.0$ leaves the fraction of $Q$ unchanged, so any change in the fraction is wrong.

recognize.clues: Two operands are given as 32-bit hex words and the product must be given as a hex word, so fields must be decoded, combined and re-packed with a bias.
recognize.contrast: This is multiplication, not addition: no exponent alignment or significand shift is needed, which is why a power-of-two operand makes the fraction pass through unchanged.

check.body: Check the magnitude. The value of Q is about 0.86009 and P is -16, so the product should be about -13.76. Decode option C: sign negative, exponent field 130 gives $2^3$, significand $1.f = 2 \times 0.86009 = 1.72018$, so the value is about $-13.76$. questions.stem: Let R1 and R2 be two 4-bit registers that store numbers in 2’s complement form. For the operation R1 + R2, which one of the following values of R1 and R2 gives an arithmetic overflow?

steps.title: Define the range and the overflow rule
steps.body: Two's complement with $n$ bits stores an integer $v$ as the bit pattern of $v \bmod 2^n$. The leftmost bit has weight $-2^{n-1}$ and every other bit $+2^i$, so the representable values are exactly $-2^{n-1}$ to $2^{n-1}-1$. Overflow means the true arithmetic result falls outside that range, so the $n$-bit pattern would show a wrong value. With 4 bits the range is $-8$ to $+7$. steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only pair B leaves $[-8, 7]$ (in 4 bits its pattern would read 0110, which is $+6$, a wrong sign), so option B.

shortcut.body: Both operands negative in A, B and D; only B has magnitudes summing to more than 8 ($4 + 6 = 10$). In C the sum is exactly 7, the top of the range.

traps.text: Both operands are negative and 1011 + 1110 looks large, but $-5 + (-2) = -7$ is inside $[-8, 7]$. Two negatives overflow only when their magnitudes add to more than 8.
$0011 + 0100 = 3 + 4 = 7$ is the top of the range, so it fits. Candidates see two positives whose sum is 0111 and fear a sign flip, but the sign bit is still 0.
$1001 + 1111 = -7 + (-1) = -8$ is exactly the bottom of the range. The range is asymmetric, so $-8$ is legal and this pair does not overflow.

recognize.clues: Four register pairs in 4-bit 2's complement form, and the question asks for the pair whose sum gives an arithmetic overflow, so each true sum is tested against the range.

check.body: Add the winning pair in 4 bits: 1100 + 1010 = 1 0110, and dropping the carry leaves 0110, which reads as a positive number although both operands are negative, so the sign has flipped. questions.stem: Consider three floating point numbers $A$, $B$ and $C$ stored in registers $R_A$, $R_B$ and $R_C$, respectively as per IEEE-754 single precision floating point format. steps.title: Define the decoding rule

shortcut.body: A and C differ only in the sign bit, so $A + C = 0$ without decoding. Decode $C = 12$ and $B = 36$ and note $B = 3C$ and $B - C > 0$. That leaves B, and $A + B = 24$ confirms it.

$B - C = 24 > 0$ is true. Reading the sign of $A$ and $C$ the wrong way round would make people doubt it.

questions.stem: The format of the single-precision floating-point representation of a real number as per the IEEE 754 standard is as follows: sign | exponent | mantissa. Which one of the following choices is correct with respect to the smallest normalized positive number represented using the standard?

solutionDiagram.alt: Single-precision field layout and the four options: only exponent 00000001 with an all-zero fraction is the smallest normalised positive number.

steps.title: What a normalised single-precision number is
steps.body: A single-precision word has 32 bits: 1 sign bit $S$, 8 exponent bits $E$ and 23 fraction bits $F$ (the question calls them the mantissa). Read $E$ as an ordinary unsigned number from 0 to 255. A normalised number is one with $1 \le E \le 254$, and it means $(-1)^S \times 1.F \times 2^{E-127}$, where the 1 in front of the point is not stored but always understood. The exponent pattern $E = 0$ is reserved: with $F = 0$ it means the number zero, and with $F \ne 0$ it means a subnormal number, which has no understood 1. $E = 255$ is reserved for infinity and NaN. The rule that decides the question: a normalised number must have $E \ge 1$.

steps.title: Throw out the options with exponent 00000000
steps.body: Options A and B have $E = 0$, so neither is normalised. Option A is the number zero, which is not positive. Option B is a subnormal number worth $2^{-23} \times 2^{-126} = 2^{-149}$. It is the smallest positive number of all, but the question asks for the smallest normalised one.

steps.title: Compare C and D
steps.body: Both have $E = 00000001 = 1$, so the power of two is $1 - 127 = -126$. In C the fraction is all zeros, so the value is $1.0 \times 2^{-126}$. In D the last fraction bit is 1, so the value is $(1 + 2^{-23}) \times 2^{-126}$, which is slightly larger. With the exponent fixed, a smaller fraction gives a smaller number, so C is smaller.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The smallest normalised positive number has exponent 00000001 and an all-zero fraction, which is option C.

shortcut.body: Smallest normalised means the smallest allowed exponent and the smallest fraction. Allowed exponents start at 1, not 0, because 0 is taken by zero and subnormals. So the exponent is 00000001 and the fraction is all zeros. Any option with exponent 00000000 can be struck out on sight.

traps.text: Exponent 0 and fraction 0 is the smallest bit pattern, but it stands for the number zero. It is not positive and not normalised.
Exponent 0 with the lowest fraction bit set is the smallest positive number the format can hold, $2^{-149}$. It is subnormal, and the question asks for the smallest normalised number.

Candidates think a positive number needs a nonzero fraction. The understood leading 1 already makes the value positive, so the fraction can stay all zeros, and a fraction of 0...01 only makes the value larger.

recognize.clues: The words "smallest normalized positive" together with exponent and mantissa bit patterns in the options point to the extreme-value rules for the single-precision format.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse it with the smallest positive number at all, which is subnormal with exponent 0 and a fraction of one. "Normalized" removes that pattern.

check.body: The largest subnormal number is $(1 - 2^{-23}) \times 2^{-126}$, which is just below $2^{-126}$. So the first normal number sits directly above all the subnormals and nothing normal can be smaller. A bit-pattern check agrees: the pattern with exponent 1 and fraction 0 is the integer 0x00800000, the first word after the subnormals.

steps.title: Binary fractions and the rule for equal numerals
steps.body: After the point, the digits of a binary numeral have weights $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac1{16}, \dots$ (each is half the one before). After the point in a decimal numeral the weights are $\tfrac1{10}, \tfrac1{100}, \dots$. Two numerals are equal when they name the same number, and a decimal numeral that does not end in an endless run of 9s is the only decimal numeral for its number. So the plan is to find the decimal value of $(0.1101)_2$ and read off its digits.

steps.title: Evaluate (0.1101) in binary
steps.body: The bits are 1, 1, 0, 1 with weights $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac1{16}$. The third bit is 0, so it adds nothing.

steps.title: Match the digits with 0.8xy5
steps.body: The decimal numeral $0.8125$ has digits 8, 1, 2, 5 after the point. The pattern $0.8xy5$ has digits 8, $x$, $y$, 5. Matching place by place gives $x = 1$ and $y = 2$, so $x + y = 3$.

shortcut.body: Learn that $\tfrac1{16} = 0.0625$. Then $0.1101$ in binary is $0.5 + 0.25 + 0.0625 = 0.8125$ in one line, and the digits are read straight off. The same trick works for any four-bit fraction: the value is the integer $1101_2 = 13$ divided by 16.

traps.text: Answer 13: the bits 1101 were read as the whole number 13 and the point was ignored. The value has to be divided by 16 to get 0.8125.

Answer 7: the digits of 0.8125 were lined up with the end of the pattern, so $x = 2$ and $y = 5$. The last 5 in the pattern is fixed, so $x$ and $y$ are the two digits between 8 and 5, which are 1 and 2.

recognize.clues: A binary fraction equated to a decimal fraction with two unknown digits means converting a fractional part between bases and matching digits.
recognize.contrast: Not an integer base change by repeated division: for a fractional part you add weights going right (or multiply by the radix going the other way), and the position of each digit matters.

check.body: Multiply the decimal value back: $0.8125 \times 16 = 13$, and 13 is 1101 in binary, the given bits. Also plug in the digits: $0.8xy5$ with $x = 1$ and $y = 2$ reads 0.8125, which is the value just found.

questions.stem: If the numerical value of a 2-byte unsigned integer on a little endian computer is 255 more than that on a big endian computer, which of the following choices represent(s) the unsigned integer on a little endian computer?

solutionDiagram.alt: The two bytes of each option placed at addresses 0 and 1 and read as little endian and as big endian: options A and D differ by plus 255, options B and C by minus 255.

steps.title: Bytes, significance and the two byte orders
steps.body: A 2-byte unsigned integer is stored in two memory cells with consecutive addresses. One byte is the high byte $H$ (weight 256) and the other is the low byte $L$ (weight 1), so the number is $256H + L$ with $0 \le H, L \le 255$. A little endian computer puts the low byte at the lower address. A big endian computer puts the high byte at the lower address. So the same two bytes in memory are read as two different numbers by the two machines. The question compares those two readings of the same memory contents.

steps.title: Write the difference as an equation
steps.body: Let the little endian value be $256H + L$, so memory holds $L$ at address 0 and $H$ at address 1. A big endian computer reads address 0 as its high byte, so it sees $256L + H$. The little endian value is 255 more exactly when the difference is 255.

steps.title: Test each option as the little endian value
steps.body: The high byte is the first two hex digits and the low byte is the last two. (A) 0x6665: $H = 0x66 = 102$, $L = 0x65 = 101$, $H - L = 1$. Yes: little endian 26213, big endian 0x6566 = 25958, difference 255. (B) 0x0001: $H = 0$, $L = 1$, $H - L = -1$, so the difference is $-255$. No. (C) 0x4243: $H = 66$, $L = 67$, $H - L = -1$. No. (D) 0x0100: $H = 1$, $L = 0$, $H - L = 1$. Yes: little endian 256, big endian 1.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Options A and D satisfy $H - L = 1$, so the answer is A and D.

shortcut.body: Swap the two bytes of each option to get the other machine's reading, and keep the option only if the first byte is exactly one more than the second: 66 and 65 fit, 01 and 00 fit, 00 and 01 do not, 42 and 43 do not. This takes about a minute and does not need any decimal conversion.

traps.text: 0x0001 against 0x0100 differ by 255 in size, so it looks right. But 0x0001 is the little endian value here, and it is the smaller of the two, so the little endian number is 255 less, not more.

0x4243 has two neighbouring bytes (the letters B and C), which suggests a difference of one. The high byte is smaller than the low byte, so the little endian value is 255 less than the big endian one.

Leaving out D is a common slip: 0x0100 looks like an odd choice, but with $H = 1$ and $L = 0$ it satisfies $H - L = 1$ exactly. Both A and D must be marked, because an MSQ scores only when the whole set is right.

recognize.clues: The words little endian, big endian and "255 more" on a 2-byte unsigned integer point to the two bytes keeping their weights 256 and 1 while swapping places between the machines.
recognize.contrast: Base conversion rewrites one value in another base; here the digits stay the same and only their weights change with the byte order, so the difference of the two readings is the equation to solve.

check.body: Test the identity on a pair that is not among the options. 0x0302 is 770 and its byte swap 0x0203 is 515, a difference of 255, with $H - L = 1$ again. A pair with $H - L = 2$, such as 0x0301 = 769 against 0x0103 = 259, differs by 510. So only $H - L = 1$ gives 255, whatever the size of the bytes, and the sign of $H - L$ decides plus or minus.

questions.stem: Let the representation of a number in base 3 be 210. What is the hexadecimal representation of the number?

solutionDiagram.alt: Base 3 digits 2, 1, 0 with weights 9, 3, 1 give 21, and 21 is 1 times 16 plus 5, which is 15 in hexadecimal.

steps.title: Positional value and changing base
steps.body: In base $r$ a numeral $d_k \dots d_1 d_0$ has the value $\sum d_i\, r^i$: the rightmost digit counts ones, the next counts $r$ each, the next $r^2$ each, and so on. Every digit is less than $r$. To change base, first find the value as an ordinary number, then write that number in the new base by repeated division. A numeral does not change its value when it is shown in another base, only its digits do.

steps.title: Value of (210) in base 3
steps.body: The digits 2, 1, 0 have weights $3^2 = 9$, $3^1 = 3$ and $3^0 = 1$.

steps.title: Write 21 in base 16
steps.body: Divide by 16: $21 = 1 \cdot 16 + 5$, so the quotient 1 is the left digit and the remainder 5 is the right digit. Both are below 16, so they are written as the hex digits 1 and 5.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The hexadecimal representation is 15, which is option A.

shortcut.body: Base 3 digits 2, 1, 0 give 18 + 3 + 0 = 21 in a few seconds. 21 is one sixteen and five, so hex 15. A quick check on the options: 21 is 0x15 only, since the digits of 0x21 would make 33.

traps.text: 21 is the right value but in decimal. The question asks for hexadecimal, and 0x21 would be 33, so the value has to be converted once more.
D2 is 210 written in hexadecimal. It comes from reading 210 as the decimal number and forgetting that the digits are base 3.
528 is the decimal value of 0x210. It comes from reading the digits 210 as hexadecimal, so the base 3 meaning is ignored altogether.

recognize.clues: A short numeral with its base named (base 3) and a different target base (hexadecimal), with no fraction or sign, points to the chain of finding the value and then dividing by the new base.
recognize.contrast: unknown-radix has the base itself as the unknown, found from an equation; here both bases are given, so no equation is needed.

check.body: Convert back. Hex 15 is $1\cdot 16+5=21$. Writing 21 in base 3 gives $2\cdot 9+1\cdot 3+0$, the digits 2, 1, 0 of the original numeral, so the round trip returns the given number.

questions.stem: Consider the following representation of a number in IEEE 754 single-precision floating point format with a bias of 127. $S: 1$, $E: 10000001$, $F: 11110000000000000000000$. Here $S$, $E$ and $F$ denote the sign, exponent and fraction components of the floating point representation. The decimal value corresponding to the above representation (rounded to 2 decimal places) is ____.

solutionDiagram.alt: The fields S = 1, E = 10000001 and F = 1111 followed by zeros are decoded to exponent 2 and significand 1.9375, giving minus 7.75.

steps.title: How a single-precision word is read
steps.body: A normalised single-precision number has a sign bit $S$ (1 means negative), an 8-bit exponent field $E$ read as an unsigned number, and a 23-bit fraction $F$. The exponent is stored with a bias of 127, so the true power of two is $E - 127$. The fraction has an understood 1 in front of the point, so the significand is $1.F$ in binary. The rule is the formula below.

steps.title: Decode the exponent and the sign
steps.body: $S = 1$, so the number is negative. $E = 10000001_2 = 128 + 1 = 129$, so the power of two is $129 - 127 = 2$.

steps.title: Decode the significand
steps.body: $F$ starts 1111 and then has only zeros, so the significand is $1.1111_2$. The weights after the point are $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac1{16}$.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: The value is the sign times the significand times $2^2$.

shortcut.body: Shift the point instead of multiplying: the exponent 129 - 127 = 2 moves the point two places right, so 1.1111 becomes 111.11 = 7.75. The sign bit is 1, so the answer is -7.75. Watch for the understood 1 and the sign; those are where marks are lost.

traps.text: 7.75 without the minus sign: the sign bit S = 1 was read but not applied. It means negative.
-3.75: the understood leading 1 was left out, so the significand became 0.9375 instead of 1.9375 and 0.9375 times 4 gave 3.75 (the sign applied).
-3.875: the exponent 129 was biased by 128 instead of 127, giving a power of 1 instead of 2, and 1.9375 times 2 is 3.875. The bias of single precision is 127.

recognize.clues: The three fields S, E and F are given as bit strings with a bias of 127 and the question asks for the decimal value, so the task is to decode a normalised single-precision word.
recognize.contrast: ieee754-special covers an exponent field of all zeros or all ones; here E is 10000001, neither extreme, so the normal decode formula with the understood 1 applies.

check.body: Bounds check and point shift. An unbiased exponent of 2 puts the magnitude in the interval from 4 to 8, and the sign bit makes it negative. Moving the point two places right in 1.1111 gives 111.11, which is $4+2+1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14$ and lies inside that interval.

questions.stem: Consider three registers R1, R2, and R3 that store numbers in IEEE-754 single precision floating point format. Assume that R1 and R2 contain the values (in hexadecimal notation) 0x42200000 and 0xC1200000, respectively. If $R3 = \frac{R1}{R2}$, what is the value stored in R3?

solutionDiagram.alt: R1 decodes to plus 40 and R2 to minus 10, so R3 is minus 4, which is sign 1, exponent 10000001, fraction zero, or 0xC0800000.

steps.title: The single-precision format and the rule for decoding
steps.body: A single-precision word has 1 sign bit $S$, 8 exponent bits $E$ and 23 fraction bits $F$. A hex digit is 4 bits, so 8 hex digits fill the 32 bits, with the sign bit as the top bit of the first digit. The value is $(-1)^S \times 1.F \times 2^{E-127}$: the exponent is biased by 127 and there is an understood 1 before the point. To divide, decode both numbers, divide as ordinary numbers, and encode the quotient with the same rule in reverse.

steps.title: Decode R1 = 0x42200000
steps.body: In binary, 0x42200000 is 0100 0010 0010 0000 0000 .... So $S = 0$, $E = 1000\,0100 = 132$ and the fraction starts 01 and then has zeros. The power of two is $132 - 127 = 5$ and the significand is $1.01_2 = 1.25$.

steps.title: Decode R2 = 0xC1200000
steps.body: In binary, 0xC1200000 is 1100 0001 0010 0000 0000 .... So $S = 1$, $E = 1000\,0010 = 130$ and the fraction again starts 01. The power of two is $130 - 127 = 3$ and the significand is $1.25$.

steps.title: Divide and encode the quotient
steps.body: $R3 = 40 / (-10) = -4 = -1.0 \times 2^2$. The sign bit is 1, $E = 2 + 127 = 129 = 1000\,0001$ and the fraction is all zeros. Writing 1 | 10000001 | 000... in groups of four gives 1100 0000 1000 0000 0000 ..., which is 0xC0800000, option B.

shortcut.body: Skip the fraction bits: 0x4220 and 0xC120 differ only in the sign and the exponent, and both fractions are 1.25. So R1/R2 = -(1.25 x 32)/(1.25 x 8) = -4. The result is negative, so the top hex digit is 8 to F, and a magnitude of 4 is 2^2 with E = 129, which starts 0xC08. This is unsafe only if the fractions differ.

traps.text: 0x40800000 is +4. It has the right magnitude but the sign is lost: dividing a positive by a negative gives a negative result, and the sign bit has to be 1.
0x83400000 has an exponent field of 00000110, so it is a tiny negative number near $2^{-121}$. Its exponent is nowhere near the biased value 129 that a magnitude of 4 needs.
0xC8500000 has an exponent field of 144, so it is about $-2\times 10^5$. A quick look at the exponent shows it is far too big for a quotient of 40 by 10.

recognize.clues: Registers are given as hex words in single precision and the result of a division must be written back as a hex word, so the work is decode, compute, then encode.
recognize.contrast: fp-range-precision asks how large or fine the format can go; here every value is small and exact, so no rounding or range question arises.

check.body: Decode the result back and multiply. 1 10000001 000... has $S=1$, $E=129$ and fraction zero, so it is $-1\times 2^{2}=-4$. Then $R2\times R3=(-10)(-4)=40$, which is the value of R1, so dividing R1 by R2 gives R3.

questions.stem: In 16-bit 2's complement representation, the decimal number $-28$ is:

solutionDiagram.alt: Minus 28 in 16-bit 2's complement: write 28 as 0000 0000 0001 1100, flip every bit, add 1 to reach 1111 1111 1110 0100.

steps.title: What 2's complement means
steps.body: In $n$-bit 2's complement the leftmost bit has weight $-2^{n-1}$ and every other bit has its usual positive weight $2^i$. A negative number $-m$ is stored as the bit pattern of $2^n - m$. Doing that by hand is easy: write $m$ in $n$ bits, flip every bit (this gives $2^n - 1 - m$), then add 1.

steps.title: Flip every bit, then add 1
steps.body: Flipping gives 1111 1111 1110 0011. Adding 1 turns the final 0011 into 0100, with no carry beyond that, so the result is 1111 1111 1110 0100 (0xFFE4).

steps.title: Check against the options
steps.body: As a check, 0xFFE4 = 65508, and $65508 - 65536 = -28$. That matches option C.

shortcut.body: Take 28 = 0001 1100 in 8 bits. Flip to 1110 0011 and add 1 to get 1110 0100 (0xE4). To reach 16 bits, copy the sign bit 1 into the new high byte: 1111 1111 1110 0100. This is option C. You can also check which options end in ...0100 and begin with 1s.

traps.text: 1111 1111 0001 1100 puts the sign bits in front of the plain pattern of 28 (0001 1100) without flipping. It is $-228$, not $-28$.
0000 0000 1110 0100 is the 8-bit pattern of $-28$ (0xE4) padded with zeros. A zero-padded pattern is positive, here $+228$. The top bits must copy the sign bit.
1000 0000 1110 0100 is the 8-bit pattern of $-28$ with a sign bit set over zero padding. In 16-bit 2's complement that is $-32540$.

recognize.clues: A negative decimal number and a fixed 16-bit width with the words 2's complement ask for the bit pattern, so the invert-and-add-one method applies.
recognize.contrast: signed-representations also covers sign-magnitude, which flips only the sign bit; the phrase 2's complement selects inversion of all bits plus one.

check.body: Add the magnitude back. 1111 1111 1110 0100 + 0000 0000 0001 1100 gives 1 0000 0000 0000 0000, and the carry out of the 16th bit is dropped, leaving zero. A pattern and its negative must sum to zero.

questions.stem: Consider $Z = X - Y$, where $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are all in sign-magnitude form. $X$ and $Y$ are each represented in $n$ bits. To avoid overflow, the representation of $Z$ would require a minimum of:

solutionDiagram.alt: For n equal to 4 the operands lie in minus 7 to 7 and X minus Y in minus 14 to 14, which fits in 5-bit sign-magnitude (minus 15 to 15) but not 4-bit.

steps.title: Sign-magnitude and overflow
steps.body: A sign-magnitude number keeps one bit for the sign (0 for plus, 1 for minus) and uses all the other bits for the size of the number as an unsigned magnitude. With $m$ magnitude bits the magnitude can be $0$ to $2^m - 1$, and the range is $-(2^m - 1)$ to $+(2^m - 1)$. Overflow means the true result lies outside the range of the width used. The task is to find the smallest width whose range holds every possible value of $X - Y$.

steps.title: Range of X and Y
steps.body: With $n$ bits there are $n - 1$ magnitude bits, so $X$ and $Y$ each lie in $[-(2^{n-1} - 1),\ 2^{n-1} - 1]$.

steps.title: Range of X - Y
steps.body: The largest difference is the largest $X$ minus the smallest $Y$, and the smallest difference is the opposite. So $Z$ can reach $\pm(2^{n} - 2)$.

steps.title: Count the bits for Z
steps.body: With $n - 1$ magnitude bits the largest magnitude is $2^{n-1} - 1$, which is too small for $2^n - 2$ once $n \ge 2$. With $n$ magnitude bits the largest magnitude is $2^n - 1 \ge 2^n - 2$, which is enough. Add one sign bit: $n + 1$ bits in total. That is option C.

shortcut.body: Subtracting two numbers of size up to M gives a result up to 2M, and doubling a magnitude costs exactly one more bit. The sign bit is still just one bit, so the total grows by 1: n + 1. A tiny case confirms it: n = 4 gives X, Y in [-7, 7], X - Y in [-14, 14], and 5 bits hold up to 15.

traps.text: n bits is enough only for the sum of numbers of opposite sign or for the difference of numbers of the same sign. In the worst case, X - Y with X large and positive and Y large and negative, the magnitude doubles and n bits overflow.
n - 1 bits is even narrower than the operands themselves. Such a width cannot hold X or Y, so it cannot hold their difference either.
n + 2 bits would also hold the result, but it is more than needed. The magnitude of X - Y needs only one more bit than the operands' magnitudes, and the question asks for the minimum.

recognize.clues: Both operands and the result are in sign-magnitude form, the operand width is $n$, and the question asks for the minimum width of the result, so the sign bit and the magnitude bits are counted separately.
recognize.contrast: add-sub-overflow tests a result against a fixed two's complement range; here the width itself is the unknown, so the worst-case magnitude is what to size.

check.body: Test a small width by listing values. For $n=3$ the operands lie in $[-3, 3]$, so $X-Y$ reaches $\pm 6$. A 3-bit sign-magnitude word stops at 3, while a 4-bit one reaches 7, so one extra bit is needed and enough.

questions.stem: Consider the unsigned 8-bit fixed point binary number representation below, $b_7 b_6 b_5 b_4 b_3 . b_2 b_1 b_0$, where the position of the binary point is between $b_3$ and $b_2$. Assume $b_7$ is the most significant bit. Some of the decimal numbers listed below cannot be represented exactly in the above representation: (i) 31.500 (ii) 0.875 (iii) 12.100 (iv) 3.001. Which one of the following statements is true?
options: None of (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) can be exactly represented
Only (iii) and (iv) cannot be exactly represented
Only (i) and (ii) cannot be exactly represented

solutionDiagram.alt: Weights of the eight bits of the 5.3 fixed point format and a verdict for each number: 31.500 and 0.875 are multiples of one eighth, 12.100 and 3.001 are not.

steps.title: What fixed point means and what it can store
steps.body: In a fixed point format the binary point sits at a fixed place, so the stored bits are just a whole number $k$ and the value is $k \times 2^{-f}$, where $f$ is the number of bits after the point. Here $f = 3$ (bits $b_2 b_1 b_0$), and the five bits $b_7 \dots b_3$ count whole units. The weights are $16, 8, 4, 2, 1$ before the point and $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18$ after it. So the stored values are exactly the multiples of $\tfrac18$ from 0 to $\tfrac{255}{8} = 31.875$. A decimal number is represented exactly when $8x$ is a whole number between 0 and 255.

steps.title: Test the four numbers
steps.body: (i) $8 \times 31.5 = 252$: a whole number in range, exact (11111.100). (ii) $8 \times 0.875 = 7$: exact (00000.111). (iii) $8 \times 12.1 = 96.8$: not whole, so 12.100 cannot be stored. (iv) $8 \times 3.001 = 24.008$: not whole, so 3.001 cannot be stored.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (iii) and (iv) cannot be represented exactly, which is option C.

shortcut.body: The fraction part must be a multiple of 0.125, so it has to be one of .000, .125, .250, .375, .500, .625, .750, .875. Check the fraction of each number: .500 yes, .875 yes, .100 no, .001 no. Integer parts 31, 0, 12, 3 all fit in 5 bits. This takes under a minute.

traps.text: Believing no decimal fraction can be stored exactly in binary. That is only true for fractions like 0.1 whose denominator has a factor other than 2. Fractions such as .5 and .875 are sums of powers of two and are exact.
Claiming 0.875 cannot be stored. It equals $\tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18$, which uses all three fraction bits, so it fits exactly.
Saying 31.500 does not fit because 31.5 is close to 32. The integer part 31 is 11111, which five bits hold, and .5 is the first fraction bit, so it fits exactly.

recognize.clues: The format is drawn as bits with a fixed binary point between $b_3$ and $b_2$, and the question lists decimal values to test for exact storage, so the fixed spacing of the format decides each one.
recognize.contrast: ieee754-format moves the point with an exponent, so its spacing changes with size; here the spacing is the same everywhere, which is why one multiple-of test settles every number.

check.body: Write the binary forms. 31.5 is 11111.100 and 0.875 is 00000.111, both inside the eight bits. For 12.1 the fraction 0.1 is 0.000110011... in binary and never ends, so three fraction bits can reach only 12.000 or 12.125, and 12.100 sits between them.

questions.stem: The representation of the value of a 16-bit unsigned integer $X$ in hexadecimal number system is BCA9. The representation of the value of $X$ in octal number system is

solutionDiagram.alt: Hex digits B, C, A, 9 expanded to sixteen bits and regrouped in threes from the right into the octal digits 1, 3, 6, 2, 5, 1.

steps.title: Why binary is the bridge between hex and octal
steps.body: Hex is base $2^4$, so one hex digit is exactly 4 bits. Octal is base $2^3$, so one octal digit is exactly 3 bits. Because both are powers of 2, converting between them needs no arithmetic: expand each hex digit to 4 bits, then regroup the same bits in threes. The grouping must start at the right end, the end of the number with the units place, because the weights $8^j = 2^{3j}$ line up with bit positions counted from the right. The leftmost group may be shorter.

steps.title: Regroup in threes from the right
steps.body: The 16 bits split as 1 | 011 | 110 | 010 | 101 | 001, with a single bit on the far left because 16 is not a multiple of 3. The groups are 1, 3, 6, 2, 5, 1.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The octal representation is 136251, which is option D.

shortcut.body: Write the binary, then draw group lines from the right: 1|011|110|010|101|001. The six digits are 1 3 6 2 5 1. A quick elimination: the value is below 65536 = 2^16, and the top octal digit of a 16-bit number is 0 or 1, so options starting with 5 or 7 are out immediately.

traps.text: 571244 comes from grouping the bits in threes from the left and padding the last group with zeros: 101 111 001 010 100 1 becomes 5 7 1 2 4 4. The grouping must start at the right.
736251 groups from the right but fills the short leftmost group 1 with ones (111 = 7) instead of leaving it as 001 = 1. Missing places are filled with zeros.
571247 groups from the left like option A and then pads the last group with ones, so the last digit becomes 7. Both slips come from not starting at the units end.

recognize.clues: Both bases are powers of 2 (16 and 8) and the number is given as a 16-bit pattern in hex, so regrouping its bits converts it with no arithmetic.
recognize.contrast: Going through decimal and dividing by 8 also works but is slow and error-prone; the power-of-2 relation makes the bit regrouping exact.

check.body: Compare decimal values. BCA9 in hex is $11\cdot 4096+12\cdot 256+10\cdot 16+9=48297$. Reading 136251 in octal gives $32768+12288+3072+128+40+1=48297$, the same number.

questions.stem: Given the following binary number in 32-bit (single precision) IEEE-754 format: 00111110011011010000000000000000. The decimal value closest to this floating-point number is

solutionDiagram.alt: The 32 bits split as sign 0, exponent 01111100 equal to 124, and fraction 1101101 then zeros, decoded to 1.8515625 times 2 to the minus 3, about 0.2314.

steps.title: The fields and the decoding rule
steps.body: A single-precision number has 1 sign bit $S$, 8 exponent bits $E$ and 23 fraction bits $F$, counted from the left. For a normalised number the value is $(-1)^S \times 1.F \times 2^{E-127}$, where 127 is the bias subtracted from the stored exponent and the 1 before the point is understood, not stored. Count the fields first, then compute.

steps.title: Split the 32 bits
steps.body: 0 | 01111100 | 11011010000000000000000. The sign is 0, so the number is positive. The exponent field is $01111100_2 = 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 124$, so the power of two is $124 - 127 = -3$.

steps.title: Evaluate the significand
steps.body: The fraction is 1101101 followed by zeros, so the significand is $1.1101101_2$. The weights after the point are $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \dots$, and the bits are 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1.

steps.title: Scale and pick the closest option
steps.body: The value is $1.8515625 \times 2^{-3} = 1.8515625 / 8 \approx 0.2314$. The options are 14.5, 0.145, 0.227 and 22.7. The distances from 0.2314 are 14.27, 0.086, 0.004 and 22.47, so the closest is $2.27 \times 10^{-1}$, option C.

shortcut.body: Only the size matters because the options are far apart. The exponent field is 124, so the power is -3 and the number is about 8 times smaller than its significand. The significand is between 1 and 2 (here about 1.85). So the value is about 1.85/8 = 0.23. Only 2.27 x 10^-1 is of that size.

traps.text: 14.5 is about $1.85 \times 2^3$. It comes from taking the exponent as $+3$ instead of $124 - 127 = -3$, a sign slip when removing the bias.
0.145 is nearest to the answer if the understood 1 is left out: $0.8515625 / 8 \approx 0.106$. The hidden bit must be added back, giving 1.85.
22.7 is the correct digits 2.27 with the decimal point shifted by two places. The size of the number is set by $2^{-3}$, so a result near 23 is far too big.

recognize.clues: A 32-bit string given in binary and the phrase "single precision IEEE-754" ask for the decimal value, so the bits must be split into sign, exponent and fraction and decoded.
recognize.contrast: ieee754-format only names the fields and the bias; here the work is the full decode, and the options are far apart, so a size estimate from the exponent alone already separates them.

check.body: Second route by magnitude: the exponent field 124 is 3 below the bias 127, so the number is the significand in $[1,2)$ divided by 8, namely about $1.85/8$. Re-encode 0.2314: it lies between $2^{-3}=0.125$ and $2^{-2}=0.25$, so its stored exponent must be $-3+127=124$, which matches the given field.

questions.stem: Consider a quadratic equation $x^2 - 13x + 36 = 0$ with coefficients in a base $b$. The solutions of this equation in the same base $b$ are $x = 5$ and $x = 6$. Then $b =$ ____.

steps.title: A numeral in an unknown base
steps.body: In base $b$ a two-digit numeral $d_1 d_0$ means $d_1 b + d_0$. So $13$ in base $b$ means $b + 3$ and $36$ in base $b$ means $3b + 6$. The digits 5 and 6 are single digits, so they have the same value in every base larger than 6, and base $b$ needs $b \ge 7$ because the digit 6 appears. Then the equation is an ordinary quadratic whose coefficients depend on $b$.

steps.title: Use the sum and the product of the roots
steps.body: For $x^2 - sx + p = 0$ the roots add to $s$ and multiply to $p$. The roots are 5 and 6, so the sum is 11 and the product is 30. Setting these equal to the coefficients gives two equations.

steps.title: Solve and check
steps.body: The first equation gives $b = 8$. The second gives $3b = 24$, so $b = 8$ too, and the two agree. In base 8 the equation is $x^2 - 11x + 30 = 0$ in decimal terms, and $x = 5$ gives $25 - 55 + 30 = 0$, $x = 6$ gives $36 - 66 + 30 = 0$. The digits used (1, 3, 6, 5) are all below 8, so base 8 is valid.

shortcut.body: Add the roots: 5 + 6 = 11 must equal the coefficient 13 in base b, which is b + 3. So b = 8. A single equation is enough; the product 30 = 3b + 6 is only a check, and it agrees.

traps.text: Answer 10: the equation is read in decimal, but then the roots would add to 13, not 11, and 5 and 6 are not roots of $x^2 - 13x + 36$ in base 10.
Answers 7 or 9: the digit 13 was expanded as $b + 2$ or $b + 4$ (an off-by-one in the digit 3). The digit 3 is the units digit, so 13 in base $b$ is $b + 3$.

recognize.clues: The coefficients 13 and 36 are written in an unknown base $b$ while the roots 5 and 6 are single digits, so each numeral must be expanded by place value and then compared with sums and products of the roots.
recognize.contrast: base-conversion starts from a known base; here the base is the unknown, so the numerals become expressions in $b$ and an equation fixes $b$.

check.body: Expand from the roots instead: $(x-5)(x-6)=x^2-11x+30$. Matching this with $x^2-13_b\,x+36_b$ needs $b+3=11$ and $3b+6=30$, and both give $b=8$. Another base fails: $b=9$ would make the middle coefficient 12, not 11.

questions.stem: The $n$-bit fixed-point representation of an unsigned real number $X$ uses $f$ bits for the fraction part. Let $i = n - f$. The range of decimal values for $X$ in this representation is

solutionDiagram.alt: An n-bit unsigned fixed-point number with i integer bits and f fraction bits: all zeros is 0 and all ones is 2 to the i minus 2 to the minus f, shown for n equal to 8 and f equal to 3.

steps.title: What the fixed-point layout stores
steps.body: An unsigned fixed-point number has $i$ bits before the binary point and $f$ bits after it, so $n = i + f$. The stored bits are an unsigned whole number $k$ from 0 to $2^n - 1$, and the value is $k \times 2^{-f}$, because the lowest bit has weight $2^{-f}$. The range is therefore the smallest and largest values of $k$ scaled by $2^{-f}$.

steps.title: Smallest and largest value
steps.body: The smallest pattern is all zeros, so the minimum is 0. The largest is all ones, $k = 2^n - 1$.

steps.title: Check with an example
steps.body: For $n = 8$ and $f = 3$ we have $i = 5$. All ones is 11111.111, which is $31 + \tfrac78 = 31.875 = 32 - 0.125 = 2^5 - 2^{-3}$. The value $2^5 = 32$ itself would need a 6th integer bit. So the range is $0$ to $2^i - 2^{-f}$, option D.

shortcut.body: The smallest value is all zeros, which is 0, so options A and B (starting at the smallest nonzero step 2^-f) are out. The largest value is one step below the next power of two, 2^i, so it is 2^i - 2^-f, not 2^i. That leaves D.

traps.text: The range starting at the smallest step $2^{-f}$ is the range of the nonzero values, and the top 2^i can never be reached. The bit pattern of all zeros is a valid number and equals 0.
This has the correct top value but starts at $2^{-f}$, the smallest nonzero number. The question gives the range of values for $X$, and 0 is one of them.
Starting at 0 is right, but all ones is one step short of $2^i$. The value $2^i$ needs an extra integer bit, so it is outside this representation.

recognize.clues: The wording "unsigned", "$f$ bits for the fraction part" and "range of decimal values" asks for the extreme values of a fixed-point layout with a given split of integer and fraction bits.
recognize.contrast: twos-complement ranges run from $-2^{n-1}$ to $2^{n-1}-1$; this number is unsigned, so the minimum is 0 and no negative end appears.

check.body: Count the values instead. There are $2^n$ patterns spaced $2^{-f}$ apart starting at 0, so the largest value is $(2^n-1)\,2^{-f}$. For $n=4$, $f=1$ the patterns give 0, 0.5, 1, ..., 7.5, and $2^{3}-2^{-1}=7.5$ agrees.

questions.stem: When two 8-bit numbers $A_7 \cdots A_0$ and $B_7 \cdots B_0$ in 2's complement representation (with $A_0$ and $B_0$ as the least significant bits) are added using a ripple-carry adder, the sum bits obtained are $S_7 \cdots S_0$ and the carry bits are $C_7 \cdots C_0$. An overflow is said to have occurred if
options: all the carry bits ($C_7, \cdots, C_0$) are 1

solutionDiagram.alt: Three 8-bit additions in 2's complement: 100 plus 100 and minus 100 plus minus 100 overflow (the sign bit flips), while 100 plus minus 100 does not even though the carry out of bit 7 is 1.

steps.title: What overflow is in 2's complement
steps.body: In 8-bit 2's complement the bit 7 is the sign bit (1 means negative) and the range is $-128$ to $+127$. Overflow means the true sum is outside this range, so the 8 sum bits show a wrong number. A ripple-carry adder adds one column at a time from bit 0 up to bit 7 and passes a carry from each column to the next; $C_7$ is the carry out of the top column. Rule: two numbers of opposite sign can never overflow, because the sum lies between them. Two numbers of the same sign overflow exactly when the sum bit 7 has the other sign.

steps.title: Turn the rule into a Boolean test
steps.body: Two negatives give a positive sum: $A_7 = B_7 = 1$ and $S_7 = 0$, which is $A_7 B_7 \overline{S_7}$. Two positives give a negative sum: $A_7 = B_7 = 0$ and $S_7 = 1$, which is $\overline{A_7}\,\overline{B_7} S_7$. Either case is overflow.

steps.title: Reject A, B and D
steps.body: A is false: the carry out of bit 7 is 1 in the third example (no overflow) and 0 in the first (overflow). B is false: $-1 + (-1)$ gives 1111 1110 with every carry equal to 1, but $-2$ is in range. D looks at the least significant bits: $A_0 = B_0 = 1$ forces $S_0 = 0$, so D is true for $1 + 1 = 2$, which does not overflow. A check over all 65 536 input pairs finds that C matches true overflow on every pair, and A, B and D each fail on some pair.

shortcut.body: Overflow in 2's complement means same-sign operands and a result of the opposite sign, and the sign is bit 7, not bit 0. Only option C tests bit 7 with that pattern. If you want the carry form: overflow = C7 XOR C6 (carry into the sign column differs from the carry out), but that form is not offered here.

traps.text: The carry out of bit 7 detects overflow for unsigned numbers. For 2's complement it fails both ways: $+100 + (-100)$ has $C_7 = 1$ with no overflow, and $+100 + 100$ overflows with $C_7 = 0$.
All carries equal to 1 happens for harmless sums such as $-1 + (-1) = -2$, so it is not a test for overflow.
This has the right shape but uses bit 0 instead of bit 7. The least significant bits say nothing about the sign, so the test fires on harmless sums such as $1 + 1$.

recognize.clues: Two 8-bit 2's complement numbers added by a ripple-carry adder with named sum bits and carry bits, and the question asks when overflow occurs, so a condition on the sign bits is wanted.
recognize.contrast: Carry out of the top bit signals overflow for unsigned addition; for 2's complement the sign-bit pattern (or carry into versus carry out of the sign column) decides it, and the carry out alone is misleading.

check.body: Second route by carries: overflow equals $C_7\oplus C_6$, the carry out of the sign column differing from the carry into it. For $+100+100$ the carry into bit 7 is 1 and the carry out is 0, so overflow, matching the sign test. For $+100+(-100)$ both carries are 1, so no overflow.
